extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students, and researchers interested in the history and movements of German-language literature
extracted.subtask_description: A broad encyclopedia-style survey describing periods, movements, characteristic features, key authors, and regional scope of literature written in the German language. Useful as a reference or starting point for study or teaching.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of German literature
rubrics_metrics.description: German literature (Deutschsprachige Literatur) comprises those literary texts written in the German language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes literature written in Germany, Austria, the German parts of Switzerland and Belgium, Liechtenstein, Luxembourg, South Tyrol, and works of the German diaspora. Modern German literature is mostly in Standard German though some currents use dialects (e.g. Alemannic).

rubrics_metrics.name: Regional scope / inclusion criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: German-language literature is not limited to the nation-state of Germany but includes works from multiple countries and diasporas where German is used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly includes Austria, German parts of Switzerland and Belgium, Liechtenstein, Luxembourg, South Tyrol in Italy, and to a lesser extent the German diaspora; recognizes variation between Standard German and dialect-influenced currents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Periodization is interpretive
rubrics_metrics.description: Periodization of German literature is not an exact science; movements and periods overlap and cut-off dates are debated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article gives commonly used periods and movements (e.g., Old High German, Middle High German, Baroque, Enlightenment, Romanticism, etc.) and notes that boundaries (especially closer to the present) are more debated; medieval periods can span centuries whereas modern periods may span decades.

rubrics_metrics.name: Old High German literature characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: Early Germanic lit. up to about the mid-11th century; earliest texts include glosses, translations and adaptations of Latin Christian texts; surviving works stem from oral tradition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Famous surviving works include the Hildebrandslied and the Heliand; literature arose from missionary/pastoral translations and oral heroic verse traditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Middle High German literature features
rubrics_metrics.description: Runs from the beginning of the 12th century with a 'golden age' (1170–1230) notable for MHG lyric poetry (Minnesang), courtly romances, and a revived heroic tradition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key forms: Minnesang (courtly love lyric), rhyming couplet romances (many Arthurian), and high medieval heroic epics written in rhymed strophes (e.g., Nibelungenlied); important authors include Walther von der Vogelweide and Wolfram von Eschenbach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Baroque period aims and themes
rubrics_metrics.description: Baroque (1600–1720) was a fertile time reflecting the traumatic experience of the Thirty Years' War in poetry and prose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Genres included picaresque/adventure novels (e.g., Simplicissimus), tragedies (Trauerspiele) often on classical themes, erotic/religious/occasional poetry; literary production also included courtly novels and adaptations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Martin Opitz's prescriptive rules (Baroque)
rubrics_metrics.description: Martin Opitz established rules for the 'purity' of language, style, verse and rhyme.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These rules functioned as prescriptive stylistic standards for German Baroque poetry and verse; cited as an institutionalizing force in Baroque-era literary practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of the Reformation and translations (Early Modern)
rubrics_metrics.description: Translations and adaptations of Latin Christian texts continued into the early medieval period and the Reformation era; Martin Luther's Bible translation is highlighted in the Early New High German period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Religious translation and vernacular scripture played a formative role in shaping modern German prose and readership; the printing press and Luther's translation influenced the transition to Early New High German literature.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Enlightenment as start of modern German literature
rubrics_metrics.description: Modern literature in German begins with the authors of the Enlightenment (such as Herder).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enlightenment thinkers (e.g., Kant, Lessing, Herder) framed intellectual and cultural contexts that shaped subsequent literary movements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empfindsamkeit / Sensibility (mid-18th century)
rubrics_metrics.description: A movement (1750s–1770s) emphasizing sensibility; culminates in Goethe's Die Leiden des jungen Werthers (1774).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors associated include Klopstock and Sophie de La Roche; the movement emphasizes feeling and sensitivity as literary qualities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sturm und Drang characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: A late-1760s–early-1780s movement giving free expression to individual subjectivity and extremes of emotion as a reaction against Enlightenment rationalism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Considered ideologically linked to Johann Georg Hamann; Goethe and Schiller were notable proponents early on; the movement foregrounds intuition, emotion, and rebellion against restrictive rationalist aesthetics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weimar Classicism features
rubrics_metrics.description: Cultural and literary movement centered on Goethe and Schiller (period given as 1786–1805 or up to 1832), emphasizing classical ideals and synthesis in literature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Originated around the Weimar court cultural circle; placed in historical relation to Sturm und Drang (some practitioners moved from one to the other).

rubrics_metrics.name: German Romanticism characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: Dominant late 18th–early 19th century movement valuing humor, wit, beauty, intuition and emotion; early romantics sought a synthesis of art, philosophy and science and looked to the Middle Ages as a model of unity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Later Romanticism emphasized tensions between everyday life and supernatural/irrational creative genius; critics (e.g., Heine) challenged medieval idealization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Biedermeier context and traits
rubrics_metrics.description: Refers to literature, music, visual arts and interior design between 1815 (Congress of Vienna) and 1848, contrasting with the preceding Romantic era.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Often associated with domesticity and middle-class sensibilities; typical poets include Annette von Droste-Hülshoff and Adelbert von Chamisso.

rubrics_metrics.name: Young Germany (Junges Deutschland) features
rubrics_metrics.description: A loose youth movement (c. 1830–1850) of Vormärz writers often politically engaged and youthful in orientation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Main proponents include Karl Gutzkow, Heinrich Laube, Theodor Mundt; movement associated with political critique and the pre-1848 context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetic Realism aims (mid–late 19th century)
rubrics_metrics.description: 19th-century German Realism (Poetic Realism, 1848–1890) focused on depicting everyday life with accuracy and restraint, emphasizing the middle class, social norms, and personal morality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aimed to avoid extremes of sentimentality or revolutionary zeal, portraying quiet internal conflicts and the ironies of bourgeois life; key authors include Theodor Fontane and Adalbert Stifter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Naturalism characteristics (1880–1900)
rubrics_metrics.description: A late-19th-century movement aiming to depict life with scientific objectivity and detailed realism; emphasized environmental and hereditary determinants of behavior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Influenced by Émile Zola; rejected idealization, exposed poverty/disease/moral decay, used dialogue mimicking actual speech/dialects; prominent figures include Gerhart Hauptmann, Arno Holz, and Johannes Schlaf.

rubrics_metrics.name: 20th-century modernist movements (Expressionism, Dada, New Objectivity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Early 20th-century movements with distinct aesthetic aims (e.g., Expressionism c.1910–1920; Dada c.1914–1924; Neue Sachlichkeit/New Objectivity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These movements represent divergent responses to modernity and war; the page lists them as influential periods/forms in 20th-century German literature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kafkaesque / Kafka's thematic features
rubrics_metrics.description: Franz Kafka's writing captures themes of bureaucracy, existentialism, alienation, existential anxiety, guilt, and absurdity; 'Kafkaesque' denotes these qualities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kafka's major works (The Metamorphosis, The Trial, The Castle) are cited as exemplars; his style and themes are central to 20th-century literary discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: National Socialist era responses (exile vs internal emigration vs propaganda)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the Nazi regime some authors went into exile (Exilliteratur), others submitted to censorship or internal emigration (Innere Emigration), and National Socialist literature included propaganda and blood-and-soil themes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lists authors who exiled and those associated with inner emigration; identifies censorship and exile as defining conditions that shaped literary production and evaluation during the period.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post-war literary categories and themes
rubrics_metrics.description: Post-1945 literature includes Trümmerliteratur (rubble literature), Group 47, Holocaust literature, pop literature, and other groupings reflecting postwar experiences and debates (1945–1967 and beyond).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different national contexts (West Germany, East Germany, Austria, Switzerland) produced distinct postwar literatures; themes include reconstruction, memory, the Holocaust, and social critique (authors: Heinrich Böll, Günter Grass, Paul Celan, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: GDR (East Germany) literary scene
rubrics_metrics.description: East German literature (GDR) includes writers who negotiated state socialism, censorship, and dissidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors include Johannes R. Becher, Christa Wolf, Heiner Müller, and others; evaluation of works often considers the political/ideological and censorial context of production.

rubrics_metrics.name: Children's literature and Grimm methodology
rubrics_metrics.description: The Brothers Grimm collected and published folklore; their methodology established an early scholarly approach to collecting and recording folk stories and became the basis for folklore studies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Their Children's and Household Tales grew from 86 stories to more than 200 through revisions; the Grimms' approach is treated as a methodological standard in folklore collection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contemporary genre diversity (21st century)
rubrics_metrics.description: Contemporary German-language literature encompasses a wide range of genres — poetry (magazines), science fiction & fantasy, pop literature, migrant literature, thrillers, and novels — with many active authors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include Andreas Eschbach (SF), Benjamin von Stuckrad-Barre (pop literature), Wladimir Kaminer (migrant literature); contemporary poetry is often published in literary magazines such as DAS GEDICHT.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition as a metric (awards, Nobel Prize)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prestigious awards (e.g., the Nobel Prize in Literature) are markers of recognition for German-language authors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page notes that German-language authors have won the Nobel Prize multiple times (listing laureates) — such prizes function as an external evaluative metric in literary history studies.
